result.markdown: --- title: "Session 4 — Repeated Measures and Trajectories" subtitle: "Long format · time × arm · nested random effects · random slopes · AR(1) · missing visits · Lab 4" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - Session 3: a random intercept for **village** - Today: the **same person is measured four times** - By the end you can: - look at **trajectories** by group - fit **time × arm** with a **nested** random effect - decide on a **random slope** - fit a **GEE** with AR(1) - explain why mixed models cope with **missing visits** (MAR) ::: # Topic 1 — Looking at trajectories {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Long format ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bp |> filter(person %in% c("V01-P01", "V01-P02")) |> select(person, arm, months, sbp) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 7 × 4 person arm months sbp 1 V01-P01 Programme 0 135 2 V01-P01 Programme 3 149 3 V01-P01 Programme 6 134 4 V01-P01 Programme 12 131 5 V01-P02 Programme 0 121 6 V01-P02 Programme 3 136 7 V01-P02 Programme 6 137 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} bp |> count(person) |> count(n, name = "people") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 2 n people 1 1 7 2 2 78 3 3 241 4 4 474 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} **One row per visit** (long format) is what the models need. Only **59%** of people have all four visits. ::: ## Mean SBP by arm and visit ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} bp |> group_by(arm, months) |> summarise(mean_sbp = mean(sbp), .groups = "drop") |> ggplot(aes(months, mean_sbp, colour = arm)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) + geom_point(size = 3) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(col_blue, col_red)) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 3, 6, 12)) + labs(x = "Months", y = "Mean SBP (mmHg)", colour = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s4_repeated_measures_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=900} ::: ::: ::: {.key} Similar at baseline (randomised). The **programme arm declines** and the **control arm** stays about flat. ::: # Topic 2 — The model {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Time × arm with nested random effects ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_t <- lmer(sbp ~ months * arm + age + sex + bmi + (1 | village / person), data = bp) summary(m_t)$coefficients["months:armProgramme", ] |> round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error df t value Pr(>|t|) -0.385 0.074 2006.760 -5.197 0.000 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} The **interaction** is the **difference in slopes**: the programme arm declines **about 0.4 mmHg per month faster**. `(1 | village / person)` gives a random intercept for each village **and** for each person within it. ::: ## The effect at 12 months ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fe <- fixef(m_t) fe[["armProgramme"]] + 12 * fe[["months:armProgramme"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -4.352272 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - **arm** alone is the difference **at month 0** (near 0 after randomisation) - At 12 months: arm + 12 × interaction ≈ **−4.4 mmHg** - To get a CI for this contrast, use `emmeans` or a linear-combination function - If the trend is not a straight line, use **months as a factor** or a spline ::: ## Is the interaction within-person or between-village? ::: {.warn} The **interaction** compares **changes within people**, so the naive SE is not too small, it is **too large** (0.12 instead of 0.07). Clustering inflates SEs of **between-cluster** effects and can **reduce** them for **within-cluster** effects. That is why the model must follow the design. ::: # Topic 3 — Slopes, AR(1) and missing data {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## A random slope for time ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_s <- lmer(sbp ~ months * arm + age + sex + bmi + (1 | village) + (months | person), data = bp, control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")) anova(m_t, m_s) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Data: bp Models: m_t: sbp ~ months * arm + age + sex + bmi + (1 | village/person) m_s: sbp ~ months * arm + age + sex + bmi + (1 | village) + (months | person) npar AIC BIC logLik -2*log(L) Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq) m_t 10 21456 21516 -10718 21436 m_s 12 21460 21531 -10718 21436 0.6957 2 0.7062 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - Allows each person to have their **own trend** - The likelihood-ratio test has **p ≈ 0.7**: no evidence that trends differ: keep the **simpler** model - Random slopes need **many** visits per person; with 4 visits the model can fail to converge ::: ## GEE with AR(1) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} d <- bp |> arrange(person, months) g_ar <- geeglm(sbp ~ months * arm + age + sex + bmi, id = person, waves = months, data = d, family = gaussian, corstr = "ar1") round(summary(g_ar)$coefficients["months:armProgramme", ], 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std.err Wald Pr(>|W|) months:armProgramme -0.341 0.083 16.715 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - **Population-averaged** slope difference: about **−0.34**, close to the mixed model (**−0.39**) - **AR(1)**: correlation falls as visits are further apart - This GEE has `id = person` and so **ignores the village** level ::: ## Missing visits ::: {.key} About **13% of visits are missing**, and dropout is more likely for **older** people and after a **high** SBP. That is **missing at random** (MAR): the reason depends on **observed** values. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} complete <- bp |> group_by(person) |> filter(n() == 4) |> ungroup() c(complete_cases = n_distinct(complete$person), all_people = n_distinct(bp$person)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` complete_cases all_people 474 800 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - The **mixed model** uses **all available visits** and is valid under **MAR** if the model includes the predictors of missingness - A **complete-case** analysis drops **41% of people** and can be **biased** - If missingness depends on the **unobserved** value itself (MNAR), neither is safe: run a **sensitivity analysis** (later module) ::: ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 4 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `clustered-workshop/labs/lab4_long.R` - visits per person and a mean-by-arm plot - `months * arm` with `(1 | village / person)` - random slope, AR(1) GEE and complete cases ::: **Time:** 45 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="c4q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="936knp.dz31kc" data-show="VGhlIGRpZmZlcmVuY2UgYmV0d2VlbiBhcm1zIGluIHRoZSBjaGFuZ2UgaW4gU0JQIHBlciBt b250aA==" data-explain="VGhlIGludGVyYWN0aW9uIGlzIHRoZSBkaWZmZXJlbmNlIGluIHNsb3BlcyBiZXR3ZWVuIHRo ZSBhcm1zLiBUaGUgJ21vbnRocycgdGVybSBhbG9uZSBpcyB0aGUgY29udHJvbCBzbG9wZSwg YW5kIHRoZSBhcm0gdGVybSBhbG9uZSBpcyB0aGUgYmFzZWxpbmUgZGlmZmVyZW5jZS4="} What does the months:armProgramme coefficient in the model estimate? - The difference in mean SBP between arms at month zero - The difference between arms in the change in SBP per month - The change in SBP per month in the control arm only - The fraction of visits that are missing in the programme arm ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="c4q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="936xwg.dz3g1r" data-show="QSByYW5kb20gaW50ZXJjZXB0IGZvciB2aWxsYWdlIGFuZCBvbmUgZm9yIHBlcnNvbiB3aXRo aW4gdmlsbGFnZQ==" data-explain="VGhlIHNsYXNoIG5lc3RzIHRoZSBncm91cGluZyBmYWN0b3JzOiBwZXJzb25zIHdpdGhpbiB2 aWxsYWdlcy4gVGhpcyB0YWtlcyBhY2NvdW50IG9mIGJvdGggdGhlIHZpbGxhZ2UgbGV2ZWwg YW5kIHRoZSByZXBlYXRlZCB2aXNpdHMu"} What does (1 | village / person) specify? - Random slopes for time, estimated separately for each village and each person - A single random intercept shared by all visits of the people in a village - A fixed effect for each village and a fixed effect for each person - A random intercept for village and one for person within village ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="c4q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="937b52.dz3uj1" data-show="SXQgY29tcGFyZXMgY2hhbmdlIHdpdGhpbiBwZW9wbGUsIHdoZXJlIHRoZSBjbHVzdGVyaW5n IGNhbiBzaHJpbmsgdGhlIHZhcmlhbmNl" data-explain="QSBjb21wYXJpc29uIG9mIGNoYW5nZSB3aXRoaW4gZWFjaCBwZXJzb24gcmVtb3ZlcyB0aGUg c3RhYmxlIHBlcnNvbi10by1wZXJzb24gZGlmZmVyZW5jZXMuIENsdXN0ZXJpbmcgbWFpbmx5 IGluZmxhdGVzIGJldHdlZW4tY2x1c3RlciBlc3RpbWF0ZXMsIHN1Y2ggYXMgdGhlIGFybSBl ZmZlY3Qu"} In this model the interaction naive SE (0.12) was larger than the mixed one (0.07). What is the reason? - It compares change within people, where the clustering can shrink the variance - A mixed model gives a smaller SE than a naive model for the coefficients it estimates - Clustering increases the variance of each estimate, and this one is no different - The naive model had fewer observations available than the mixed model did ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="c4q4" data-type="mcq" data-hash="937odt.dz490g" data-show="SXQgdXNlcyBhbGwgb2JzZXJ2ZWQgdmlzaXRzLCBhbmQgZHJvcG91dCBkZXBlbmRzIG9uIHZh bHVlcyBpbiB0aGUgbW9kZWw=" data-explain="TGlrZWxpaG9vZC1iYXNlZCBtaXhlZCBtb2RlbHMgYXJlIHZhbGlkIHdoZW4gdGhlIGNoYW5j ZSBvZiBtaXNzaW5nbmVzcyBkZXBlbmRzIG9ubHkgb24gb2JzZXJ2ZWQgZGF0YSB0aGF0IGFy ZSBpbiB0aGUgbW9kZWwuIFRoZXkgZG8gbm90IG5lZWQgY29tcGxldGUgY2FzZXMu"} Under missing at random, why can the mixed model be used with incomplete follow-up? - It fills the missing visits in with the last value observed for that person - It drops everyone with a missing visit before the model is fitted to the data - It uses all observed visits, and dropout depends on values in the model - It assumes the missing visits would have had the same SBP as the observed ones ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="c4q5" data-type="mcq" data-hash="9381mh.dz4nhs" data-show="VGhlcmUgaXMgbm8gZXZpZGVuY2UgdGhhdCB0cmVuZHMgZGlmZmVyLCBzbyB0aGUgc2ltcGxl ciBtb2RlbCBpcyBrZXB0" data-explain="QSBub24tc2lnbmlmaWNhbnQgaW1wcm92ZW1lbnQgbWVhbnMgdGhlIGV4dHJhIHZhcmlhbmNl IGNvbXBvbmVudCBpcyBub3QgbmVlZGVkLiBJdCBpcyBub3QgcHJvb2Ygb2Ygbm8gZGlmZmVy ZW5jZSwgYnV0IHRoZSBzaW1wbGVyIG1vZGVsIGlzIHByZWZlcnJlZC4="} A random slope for months is tried and the likelihood-ratio p-value is 0.7. What do you conclude? - The random slope shows that the people in the trial share one identical trend - There is no evidence that trends differ, so the simpler model is kept - The model needs to be rerun with months entered as a categorical variable - The random intercept for village should now be removed from the model ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - **Long format**, one row per visit - **months × arm** = difference in slopes; `(1 | village / person)` - Within-person comparisons: SE can be **smaller** than a naive one - **Random slope** only if the data support it - **MAR**: mixed models use all visits; avoid complete cases ::: **Next:** Session 5: choosing, checking and reporting

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
